Jephthah and the elders of Gilead (verses 1–11)

People should not be blamed for their parentage when their own conduct and character remove any disgrace associated with their birth.

God had forgiven Israel, and Jephthah was therefore willing to forgive the people who had rejected him.

Jephthah did not presume that victory was certain.

He knew God could justly allow the Ammonites to succeed as a further punishment for Israel's sins.

Nor did Jephthah place confidence in himself.

If he succeeded, the Lord would have given the enemy into his hands.

In saying so, he reminded the people to look to God as the Giver of victory.

Henry applies the conversation to those who desire salvation through Christ.

If Christ saves you, will you accept him as your Ruler?

There is no salvation on terms that exclude his authority.

If he makes you happy, will you also let him make you holy?

If he becomes your Helper, will you acknowledge him as your Head?

Jephthah was willing to risk his life for a little earthly honor.

How could Christians turn away from spiritual conflict merely because it is difficult, when Christ promises the crown of life to the one who overcomes?

Jephthah seeks peace with Ammon (verses 12–28)

One way to honor God is to use our possessions rightly.

We should receive them from him, use them for him and surrender them when he calls for them.

Jephthah's message shows that he knew the books of Moses well.

His argument was clear, and his demand was reasonable.

People whose faith gives them the greatest courage are often also the most willing to pursue peace and make the first efforts to secure it.

But greed and ambition may disguise their purposes under claims of justice, making sincere attempts at peace ineffective.

Jephthah's victory and difficult vow (verses 29–40)

Henry draws five lessons from Jephthah's vow.

First, traces of distrust and uncertainty may remain even in the hearts of genuine and remarkable believers.

Second, our vows should express gratitude to God, not attempt to purchase the favor we desire.

Third, we must consider vows carefully before making them, lest they trap us.

Fourth, what we have solemnly promised to God should be done when it is possible and lawful, even if fulfilling it is painful or difficult.

Fifth, children should submit willingly and cheerfully to their parents in the Lord.

What exactly happened when Jephthah fulfilled his vow is difficult to determine.

Henry says it is thought that Jephthah did not offer his daughter as a burnt offering, because such a sacrifice would have been abhorrent to the Lord.

The proposed alternative is that she remained unmarried and lived apart from her family.

But he does not present this explanation as certain.

Learned interpreters disagree over this and several other difficult passages.

We do not need to be overwhelmed by questions whose answers are uncertain.

Thanks be to God, what is necessary for our salvation is plain.

Those who remember Christ's promise about the teaching of the Holy Spirit and submit to that heavenly Teacher will receive the truth they need to understand.

He attempts to make peace. | (12-28) |
Jephthah's vow. He vanquishes the Ammonites. | (29-40) |
Verses 1-11
Men ought not to be blamed for their parentage, so long as they by their personal merits roll away any reproach. God had forgiven Israel, therefore Jephthah will forgive. He speaks not with confidence of his success, knowing how justly God might suffer the Ammonites to prevail for the further punishment of Israel. Nor does he speak with any confidence at all in himself. If he succeed, it is the Lord delivers them into his hand; he thereby reminds his countrymen to look up to God as the Giver of victory. The same question as here, in fact, is put to those who desire salvation by Christ. If he save you, will ye be willing that he shall rule you? On no other terms will he save you. If he make you happy, shall he make you holy? If he be your helper, shall he be your Head? Jephthah, to obtain a little worldly honour, was willing to expose his life: shall we be discouraged in our Christian warfare by the difficulties we may meet with, when Christ has promised a crown of life to him that overcometh?
[Judg.11.12-Judg.11.28]
Verses 12-28
One instance of the honour and respect we owe to God, as our God, is, rightly to employ what he gives us to possess. Receive it from him, use it for him, and part with it when he calls for it. The whole of this message shows that Jephthah was well acquainted with the books of Moses. His argument was clear, and his demand reasonable. Those who possess the most courageous faith, will be the most disposed for peace, and the readiest to make advances to obtain; but rapacity and ambition often cloak their designs under a plea of equity, and render peaceful endeavours of no avail.
[Judg.11.29-Judg.11.40]
Verses 29-40
Several important lessons are to be learned from Jephthah's vow. 1. There may be remainders of distrust and doubting, even in the hearts of true and great believers. 2. Our vows to God should not be as a purchase of the favour we desire, but to express gratitude to him. 3. We need to be very well-advised in making vows, lest we entangle ourselves. 4. What we have solemnly vowed to God, we must perform, if it be possible and lawful, though it be difficult and grievous to us. 5. It well becomes children, obediently and cheerfully to submit to their parents in the Lord. It is hard to say what Jephthah did in performance of his vow; but it is thought that he did not offer his daughter as a burnt-offering. Such a sacrifice would have been an abomination to the Lord; it is supposed she was obliged to remain unmarried, and apart from her family. Concerning this and some other such passages in the sacred history, about which learned men are divided and in doubt, we need not perplex ourselves; what is necessary to our salvation, thanks be to God, is plain enough. If the reader recollects the promise of Christ concerning the teaching of the Holy Spirit, and places himself under this heavenly Teacher, the Holy Ghost will guide to all truth in every passage, so far as it is needful to be understood.

The people of Ephraim picked the same quarrel with Jephthah that they had previously picked with Gideon.

Pride lay at the bottom of it.

Pride is what so often produces strife.

It is wrong to attach insulting names to people or to entire countries, especially to those already facing outward disadvantages.

Such language can provoke quarrels with terrible consequences, as it did here.

Few disputes are more bitter than quarrels among brothers or between people competing for honor.

How carefully we need to watch and pray against sinful tempers!

May the Lord lead all his people to pursue everything that makes for peace.

Ibzan, Elon and Abdon govern Israel (verses 8–15)

This passage briefly records three more judges of Israel.

The happiest lives and the happiest condition of a community are often those that produce the fewest dramatic events for historians.

What should a wise person truly desire?

To live honorably and quietly.

To be peacefully useful to those around us.

To enjoy a clear conscience.

But above all, without which nothing else is sufficient, to enjoy fellowship with God our Savior throughout life and die at peace with both God and other people.

Samson wants to marry a Philistine woman (verses 1–4)

As an ordinary marriage decision, Samson's desire was weak and foolish.

He was not merely an Israelite; he was also a Nazirite set apart for the Lord.

Why should he seek marriage with a worshiper of Dagon?

The account gives no reason to think the woman was wise, virtuous or likely to make a good companion.

Samson simply saw something attractive in her.

Anyone who chooses a spouse solely by what the eyes see and by personal fancy has only himself to blame if the marriage proves spiritually harmful.

Still, Samson did well to speak with his parents before going further.

Henry says children ought not to marry or even begin pursuing marriage without parental counsel and consent.

Samson's parents were right to warn him against being unequally joined to someone who did not share his faith.

It seems that God allowed Samson to follow his own strong desire while intending to bring good from what happened.

His parents eventually consented because he remained determined.

But this account is not given to us as an example to imitate.

Samson kills a lion (verses 5–9)

By empowering Samson to kill the lion, God showed him what he could do through the strength given by the Lord's Spirit.

This should have encouraged him not to fear even the greatest difficulties.

Samson was alone in the vineyards after wandering away.

Young people often fail to recognize the danger they face when wandering away from wise, godly parents.

The devil is like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour.

People also fail to notice how many dangerous lions lurk in vineyards—especially where red wine and its temptations are found.

Our Lord Jesus has conquered Satan, the roaring lion.

Believers, like Samson, can therefore find honey in the defeated lion: strength and spiritual satisfaction enough for themselves and for their friends.

Literally, Samson's riddle simply meant that he had obtained honey for food and pleasure from the body of a fierce lion.

But Henry sees it as pointing toward Christ's victory over Satan.

Through Christ's humiliation, suffering and death came victory and exaltation, glory for the Father and great spiritual blessings for his people.

Even death itself, that devouring enemy, has been stripped of its sting and terror.

Instead of preventing blessedness, it now helps believers pass into eternal joy.

Thus food comes from the eater and sweetness from the strong.

Samson's companions forced his wife to obtain the answer to the riddle.

A spouse or friend who is controlled by worldly loyalties can become an enemy within the camp, always ready to betray the believer.

A close relationship cannot remain secure or happy when confidential matters cannot be shared without danger of betrayal.

Satan could not do so much harm through temptation unless he could use the corruption of our own hearts.

His greatest advantage comes from his cooperation with our deceitful desires.

This experience helped separate Samson from his new relationships.

It would be good if every disappointment and act of unkindness we experienced from the world led us, through faith and prayer, to return to our heavenly Father's house and find rest there.

Human friendship can be unreliable.

As far as Samson's marriage was a common case, it was weak and foolish of him to set his affections upon a daughter of the Philistines. Shall one, not only an Israelite, but a Nazarite, devoted to the Lord, covet to become one with a worshipper of Dagon? It does not appear that he had any reason to think her wise or virtuous, or any way likely to be a help meet for him; but he saw something in her agreeable to his fancy. He that, in the choice of a wife, is only guided by his eye, and governed by his fancy, must afterwards thank himself if he find a Philistine in his arms. Yet it was well done not to proceed till Samson had made his parents acquainted with the matter. Children ought not to marry, nor to move towards it, without the advice and consent of their parents. Samson's parents did well to dissuade him from yoking himself unequally with unbelievers. It seems that it pleased God to leave Samson to follow his own inclinations, intending to bring out good from his conduct; and his parents consented, because he was bent upon it. However, his example is not recorded for us to do likewise.
[Judg.14.5-Judg.14.9]
Verses 5-9
By enabling him to kill a lion, God let Samson know what he could do in the strength of the Spirit of the Lord, that he might never be afraid to look the greatest difficulties in the face. He was alone in the vineyards, whither he had rambled. Young people consider not how they exposed themselves to the roaring lion that seeks to devour, when they wander from their prudent, pious parents. Nor do men consider what lions lurk in the vineyards, the vineyards of red wines. Our Lord Jesus having conquered Satan, that roaring lion, believers, like Samson, find honey in the carcass abundant strength and satisfaction, enough for themselves, and for all their friends.
[Judg.14.10-Judg.14.20]
Verses 10-20
Samson's riddle literally meant no more than that he had got honey, for food and for pleasure, from the lion, which in its strength and fury was ready to devour him. But the victory of Christ over Satan, by means of his humiliation, agonies, and death, and the exaltation that followed to him, with the glory thence to the Father, and spiritual advantages to his people, seem directly alluded to. And even death, that devouring monster, being robbed of his sting, and stripped of his horror, forwards the soul to the realms of bliss. In these and other senses, out of the eater comes forth meat, and out of the strong, sweetness. Samson's companions obliged his wife to get the explanation from him. A worldly wife, or a worldly friend, is to a godly man as an enemy in the camp, who will watch every opportunity to betray him. Then he takes away their strength and honor and leads them captive.

While we sleep spiritually, our enemies remain awake.

Samson's eyes had first drawn him into sin.

Now his punishment fell upon those eyes: the Philistines blinded him.

With his physical sight gone, he had time to remember how earlier sinful desires had already blinded his judgment.

The surest way to preserve our eyes is to turn them away from worthless sights.

Let Samson's fall warn us to watch diligently against sinful physical desires.

When our consecration to God is profaned, our spiritual protection departs.

Samson's strength begins to return (verses 22–24)

Samson's suffering became the occasion for deep repentance.

Losing physical sight opened the eyes of his understanding.

After losing bodily strength, he received renewed spiritual strength from the Lord.

God sometimes permits people to wander far into sin, yet finally brings them back.

Through severe earthly consequences, he shows his displeasure at sin while keeping them from eternal ruin.

Hypocrites may misuse such stories as excuses to sin.

Unbelievers may mock them.

But faithful Christians should become more humble, cautious, watchful and dependent upon God.

They should pray more earnestly for grace to avoid falling and thank God for preserving them.

If they do fall, they should not despair of his mercy.

Samson's final prayer and death (verses 25–31)

Few actions increase a person's guilt more quickly than mocking and mistreating God's servants, even when those servants have brought disgrace upon themselves through their own folly.

Henry understands Samson as a publicly appointed judge acting under God's direction to vindicate the Lord's cause, Israel's cause and his own.

The strength Samson lost through sin was restored through prayer.

Henry argues that his action arose from holy zeal rather than merely private revenge because God accepted and answered the prayer.

The building collapsed through God's almighty power, not Samson's natural strength alone.

In this exceptional historical situation, Henry does not regard Samson as guilty of taking his own life.

He sought Israel's deliverance and the defeat of its enemies, rather than his own death.

Samson died in captivity among the Philistines—a severe correction for his sins.

Yet he died repentant.

Henry sees his death as a picture of Christ, who willingly laid down his life among transgressors, overthrew Satan's kingdom and secured deliverance for his people.

Samson's sin was great, and he deserved the judgments he brought upon himself.

Nevertheless, he found mercy at the end.

Everyone who repents and flees to Jesus Christ—the Savior whose blood cleanses from every sin—may also obtain mercy.

But nothing in Samson's story gives anyone permission to continue sinning on the assumption that repentance and salvation can be postponed until the end.

Verses 1-3
Hitherto Samson's character has appeared glorious, though uncommon. In this chapter we find him behaving in so wicked a manner, that many question whether or not he were a godly man. But the apostle has determined this, [Heb.11.32] He 11:32. By adverting to the doctrines and examples of Scripture, the artifices of Satan, the deceitfulness of the human heart, and the methods in which the Lord frequently deals with his people, we may learn useful lessons from this history, at which some needlessly stumble, while others cavil and object. The peculiar time in which Samson lived may account for many things, which, if done in our time, and without the special appointment of Heaven, would be highly criminal. And there might have been in him many exercises of piety, which, if recorded, would have reflected a different light upon his character. Observe Samson's danger. Oh that all who indulge their sensual appetites in drunkenness, or any fleshly lusts, would see themselves thus surrounded, way-laid, and marked for ruin by their spiritual enemies! The faster they sleep, the more secure they feel, the greater their danger. We hope it was with a pious resolution not to return to his sin, that he rose under a fear of the danger he was in. Can I be safe under this guilt? It was bad that he lay down without such checks; but it would have been worse, if he had laid still under them.
[Judg.16.4-Judg.16.17]
Verses 4-17
Samson had been more than once brought into mischief and danger by the love of women, yet he would not take warning, but is again taken in the same snare, and this third time is fatal. Licentiousness is one of the things that take away the heart. This is a deep pit into which many have fallen; but from which few have escaped, and those by a miracle of mercy, with the loss of reputation and usefulness, of almost all, except their souls. The anguish of the suffering is ten thousand times greater than all the pleasures of the sin.
[Judg.16.18-Judg.16.21]
Verses 18-21
See the fatal effects of false security. Satan ruins men by flattering them into a good opinion of their own safety, and so bringing them to mind nothing, and fear nothing; and then he robs them of their strength and honour, and leads them captive at his will. When we sleep our spiritual enemies do not. Samson's eyes were the inlets of his sin, (ver. #(1),) and now his punishment began there. Now the Philistines blinded him, he had time to remember how his own lust had before blinded him. The best way to preserve the eyes, is, to turn them away from beholding vanity. Take warning by his fall, carefully to watch against all fleshly lusts; for all our glory is gone, and our defence departed from us, when our separation to God, as spiritual Nazarites, is profaned.
[Judg.16.22-Judg.16.24]
Verses 22-24
Samson's afflictions were the means of bringing him to deep repentance. By the loss of his bodily sight the eyes of his understanding were opened; and by depriving him of bodily strength, the Lord was pleased to renew his spiritual strength. The Lord permits some few to wander wide and sink deep, yet he recovers them at last, and marking his displeasure at sin in their severe temporal sufferings, preserves them from sinking into the pit of destruction. Hypocrites may abuse these examples, and infidels mock at them, but true Christians will thereby be rendered more humble, watchful, and circumspect; more simple in their dependence on the Lord, more fervent in prayer to be kept from falling, and in praise for being preserved; and, if they fall, they will be kept from sinking into despair.
[Judg.16.25-Judg.16.31]
Verses 25-31
Nothing fills up the sins of any person or people faster than mocking and misusing the servants of God, even thought it is by their own folly that they are brought low. God put it into Samson's heart, as a public person, thus to avenge on them God's quarrel, Israel's, and his own. That strength which he had lost by sin, he recovers by prayer. That it was not from passion or personal revenge, but from holy zeal for the glory of God and Israel, appears from God's accepting and answering the prayer. The house was pulled down, not by the natural strength of Samson, but by the almighty power of God. In his case it was right he should avenge the cause of God and Israel. Nor is he to be accused of self-murder. He sought not his own death, but Israel's deliverance, and the destruction of their enemies. Thus Samson died in bonds, and among the Philistines, as an awful rebuke for his sins; but he died repentant. The effects of his death typified those of the death of Christ, who, of his own will, laid down his life among transgressors, and thus overturned the foundation of Satan's kingdom, and provided for the deliverance of his people. Great as was the sin of Samson, and justly as he deserved the judgments he brought upon himself, he found mercy of the Lord at last; and every penitent shall obtain mercy, who flees for refuge to that Saviour whose blood cleanses from all sin. But here is nothing to encourage any to indulge sin, from a hope they shall at last repent and be saved.

Micah and his mother turn to idols (verses 1–6)

The events described here and in the remaining chapters of Judges took place soon after Joshua died (see Judges 20:28).

The history shows how unhappy Israel could become without a judge, in contrast with the comparative peace experienced under the judges.

Love of money made Micah dishonor his mother by stealing from her.

That same love of money made his mother curse her own son.

Losses drive godly people toward prayer but can drive ungodly people toward cursing.

This woman's silver was already her god before it was shaped into a carved or cast image.

Micah and his mother agreed to turn their wealth into an idol and establish false worship in their home.

What caused this corruption?

Everyone did whatever appeared right in his own eyes.

Soon they began doing what was evil in the Lord's sight.

Micah hires a Levite as priest (verses 7–13)

Micah saw the arrival of a Levite at his house as evidence that God favored him and his idols.

This is how people can deceive themselves.

When they are already pleased with their own false beliefs, they may treat any unexpected circumstance that helps them continue in wrongdoing as proof that God approves of it.

But an apparent success in Providence is no evidence that a sinful course has become right.

Verses 1-6
What is related in this, and the rest of the chapters to the end of this book, was done soon after the death of Joshua: see chap. [Judg.20.28] Jud 20:28. That it might appear how happy the nation was under the Judges, here is showed how unhappy they were when there was no Judge. The love of money made Micah so undutiful to his mother as to rob her, and made her so unkind to her son, as to curse him. Outward losses drive good people to their prayers, but bad people to their curses. This woman's silver was her god, before it was made into a graven or a molten image. Micah and his mother agreed to turn their money into a god, and set up idol worship in their family. See the cause of this corruption. Every man did that which was right in his own eyes, and then they soon did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord.
[Judg.17.7-Judg.17.13]
Verses 7-13
Micah thought it was a sign of God's favour to him and his images, that a Levite should come to his door. Thus those who please themselves with their own delusions, if Providence unexpectedly bring any thing to their hands that further them in their evil way, are apt from thence to think that God is pleased with them.

The stolen idols of Micah

The Danites decided to take Micah's gods with them.

How foolish they were!

How could they expect those gods to protect them when the gods could not even protect themselves from being stolen?

Taking the images for their own worship was a double crime.

It showed that they neither feared God nor respected other people.

They had lost both true religion and ordinary honesty.

Micah was equally foolish.

He called objects his gods, although he himself had made them.

The only One worthy of our worship as God is the One who made us.

Whatever we value as though our whole life depended upon it has taken God's place in our hearts.

If people devoted to idols are willing to live for those false gods, how much more should we love and serve the only true God!
classic_reading:

Chapter 18
The Danites seek to enlarge their inheritance, and rob Micah.
--The Danites determined to take Micah's gods with them. Oh the folly of these Danites! How could they imagine those gods should protect them, that could not keep themselves from being stolen! To take them for their own use, was a double crime; it showed they neither feared God, nor regarded man, but were lost both to godliness and honesty. What a folly was it for Micah to call those his gods, which he had made, when He only is to be worshipped by us as God, that made us! That is put in God's place, which we are concerned about, as if our all were bound up in it. If people will walk in the name of their false gods, much more should we love and serve the true God!

The wrongdoing at Gibeah

The final three chapters of Judges tell a deeply distressing story about the wickedness of the people of Gibeah, in the tribe of Benjamin.

The righteous Lord sometimes permits sinners to carry out his just judgments against one another.

If the history described here is horrifying, how much more dreadful will be the things revealed on the day of judgment!

Every one of us should therefore consider how to escape the coming wrath.

We should put to death the sins in our own hearts, resist Satan's temptations and keep away from the pollution of the world.

Israel was right to hate the terrible crime committed at Gibeah and to resolve that those guilty of it should be punished.

But the Israelites acted too quickly and with too much confidence in themselves when they made their plans.

The destruction of most of Benjamin was dreadful.

Yet the eternal destruction of human souls is more fearful still.
